title: Excise duty and the illicit cigarette market in Brazil
gist: A British American Tobacco-commissioned Oxford Economics report on Brazil finds that steep 2010-2017 excise hikes drove the illicit cigarette market share from 26% to a peak of 57%, that stable rates from 2017-2023 partially reversed that trend, and that renewed 2024 excise increases have so far (through 2025) shown no measurable illicit-market rebound, though the report flags a one-to-three-year lag before full effects emerge.

themes.theme: 2010-2017: aggressive excise hikes fueled illicit trade

insights.claim: Between 2010 and 2017, Brazil's real price of duty-paid cigarettes rose 32% following substantial excise duty increases.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: A 32% real price rise over seven years quantifies the direct pass-through of tax policy to consumer prices, a benchmark for gauging future excise-hike impact.
insights.quote: the increase in excise duty between 2010 and 2017 was accompanied by a 32% increase in the real price of duty paid cigarettes

insights.claim: Duty-paid cigarette consumption in Brazil fell from 85 billion to 53 billion cigarettes between 2010 and 2017 as illicit consumption rose from 31 billion to 49 billion sticks.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: A roughly 38% collapse in legal volume matched almost stick-for-stick by illicit-volume growth demonstrates substitution rather than net demand destruction from the tax hikes.
insights.quote: duty paid consumption fell from 85 billion to 53 billion cigarettes, while illicit consumption increased from 31 billion to 49 billion sticks

insights.claim: Illicit cigarette consumption in Brazil continued rising after the 2010-2017 excise hikes, reaching 63 billion sticks by 2019.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: The lag between the 2017 policy shift and the 2019 illicit-volume peak illustrates that illicit-market responses to excise changes persist for years, relevant to reading the 2024 hike's eventual impact.

insights.claim: Brazil's estimated illicit cigarette market share more than doubled from 26% in 2010 to 57% in 2019 as excise duty rose sharply.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: A jump from 26% to 57% illicit share is a stark case study for how aggressive tobacco excise hikes without matched enforcement can hand majority market share to untaxed supply, relevant to tobacco-tax debates and BAT's/Brazilian legal manufacturers' volume outlook elsewhere.
insights.quote: The estimated illicit market share therefore rose from 26% in 2010 to 57% in 2019

themes.theme: 2017-2023: stable rates partially reversed illicit-market growth

insights.claim: During the 2017-2023 period of broadly stable excise rates, the price gap between legal and illicit Brazilian cigarettes narrowed and the illicit market share fell from around 48% to 37%.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: An 11-point drop in illicit share under a stable-tax regime supports the report's implicit thesis that excise-rate pauses (not just enforcement) can claw back legal-market share, a data point tobacco policymakers weighing further hikes should note.
insights.quote: illicit market share fell from around 48% to 37%

insights.claim: Tax revenues from duty-paid cigarettes in Brazil recovered during the 2017-2023 period of stable excise rates.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Revenue recovery alongside falling illicit share suggests a Laffer-curve-style dynamic in Brazilian tobacco excise policy worth citing in fiscal-policy debates on further rate hikes.
insights.quote: tax revenues from duty-paid cigarettes recovered

themes.theme: 2024 onward: renewed hikes, effects still emerging

insights.claim: Duty-paid cigarette prices in Brazil rose substantially following the 2024 excise increase, widening the price gap with illicit products.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: A widening legal-illicit price gap is the leading indicator the report uses to flag renewed illicit-market risk from the 2024 hike.
insights.quote: Duty paid cigarette prices rose substantially following the 2024 excise increase, widening the price differential with illicit products

insights.claim: As of the data available in the report, there was no measurable increase in Brazil's illicit cigarette consumption in 2025 despite the 2024 excise increase.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: The absence of an immediate illicit-market response could be read either as a policy success or as a lagging indicator that hasn't yet caught up, so it shouldn't be taken as confirmation the hike was costless.
insights.quote: the data released so far finds no measurable increase in illicit consumption in 2025

insights.claim: Consumer and illicit-supply responses to Brazilian excise changes have historically occurred with a one-to-three-year lag, meaning the full effects of the 2024 increase may not be visible until 2025-2027.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: The lag framework implies analysts and policymakers should wait through at least 2027 before declaring the 2024 hike safe from the illicit-market blowback seen after 2010-2017.
insights.quote: consumer and illicit-supply responses have historically occurred with a lag, meaning the full effects of recent tax changes may take one to three years to emerge

insights.claim: The report concludes future Brazilian excise policy needs to account for the existing illicit market, the price differential with legal cigarettes, and enforcement capacity, since higher taxes increase the economic incentive for illicit trade.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: This is effectively a policy-advocacy conclusion (from a BAT-commissioned report) that further excise hikes should be paired with enforcement funding, relevant context for evaluating the report's framing.
insights.quote: future excise policy needs to take account of the existing illicit market, price differentials and the capacity of enforcement measures to address illicit supply, particularly where higher taxes increase the economic incentives for illicit trade

insights.claim: Illicit cigarette supply into Brazil is noted to come particularly from Paraguay.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Paraguay's role as the named illicit-supply source points to cross-border enforcement and trade-policy angles as the practical lever for containing the illicit market, beyond domestic tax settings alone.
insights.quote: considers the role of illicit supply, particularly from Paraguay
